title: 12 Ukrainian Words With No English Equivalent
description: Затишок, туга, щем, доба: 12 Ukrainian words English doesn't have, with pronunciation, meaning and real examples, chosen by a native Ukrainian tutor.
h1: 12 Ukrainian words with no English equivalent
lede: Some Ukrainian words have no neat English equivalent — you can explain them, but not translate them with a single word. Here are twelve of my favourites, with pronunciation, meaning and a sentence you could actually say.

sections.h2: Why some Ukrainian words don't translate

blocks.p: Every language slices the world a little differently. English has words Ukrainian needs a whole sentence for, and Ukrainian returns the favour. When a word has no English equivalent, it usually points to something a culture has cared about for a long time: home, longing, food, and the people who are *yours*.
I've grouped the words by theme. The stressed vowel is shown in colour in the Ukrainian and with an accent in the transliteration — that's where the weight of your voice goes.

sections.h2: Words for feelings English only half-covers

blocks.h3: 1. Ту́га (túha) — longing with sorrow in it

blocks.p: *Туга* is more than missing someone. It's a heavy, aching longing — for home, for a person, for a time that's gone — with sadness woven through it. You'll find it everywhere in Ukrainian folk songs and poetry.

example.b: She was overcome by longing for home.
example.note: Туга за + instrumental: longing for someone or something.

blocks.h3: 2. Щем (shchem) — a sweet ache in the chest

blocks.p: *Щем* is the tender, slightly painful feeling you get from an old photo, a song from childhood or a view you love. The verb *щемі́ти* (shchemíty) describes the heart doing exactly that.

example.a: Від ціє́ї пі́сні аж щеми́ть у грудя́х.
example.b: This song gives me an ache in my chest.
example.note: Usually impersonal: щемить — “it aches”. The ache is bittersweet, not pain.

blocks.h3: 3. Жага́ (zhahá) — a burning thirst for something

blocks.p: Literally a fierce thirst, but mostly used figuratively: a craving so strong it drives you. Stronger than *desire*, more physical than *passion*.

example.a: У не́ї неймові́рна жага́ до життя́.
example.b: She has an incredible thirst for life.
example.note: Жага до життя is the classic pairing.

blocks.h3: 4. Спересе́рдя (speresérdya) — in a fit of annoyance

blocks.p: One word for doing or saying something rashly because you were angry or fed up — and usually regretting it afterwards. English needs a phrase: *in the heat of the moment*, *out of sheer irritation*.

example.b: He slammed the door in a fit of temper.
example.note: Спересердя is an adverb — it never changes form.

sections.h2: Words for home and the people who are yours

blocks.h3: 5. Зати́шок (zatýshok) — cosiness, shelter and calm in one

blocks.p: *Затишок* is the feeling of a warm, quiet, safe place: soft light, tea, nobody rushing you. It comes from the same root as *ти́ша* (silence), so there is always a little peace in it. *Cosiness* covers part of it; *hygge* comes closer.

example.b: I love how cosy and calm this café is.
example.note: The adverb is зати́шно: Тут так затишно! — It's so cosy here!

blocks.h3: 6. Рі́дний (rídnyi) — one's own, dear, of your blood or your heart

blocks.p: *Рідний* means native, but also *related* and *dear*. Your *рідна мова* is your mother tongue, your *рідне місто* is your home town, and your *рідні* are your relatives. Calling someone *рідна людина* means they feel like family, blood or not.

example.note: Рідний / рідна / рідне changes with gender like any adjective.

blocks.p: English has one verb for loving your partner and loving pizza. Ukrainian has two. *Люби́ти* (lyubýty) is broad: family, friends, food, music. *Кохати* is romantic love only — the love of songs and proposals.

example.note: You'd never say кохаю about coffee: Я люблю́ ка́ву — I love coffee.

blocks.p: English *day* can mean daytime or the whole 24 hours. Ukrainian has a separate word for the full cycle of day and night — and *доба* also means an era.

example.b: I didn't sleep for a whole 24 hours.
example.note: Note the stress shift: доба́, but до́бу. Also: цілодо́бово — around the clock; доба́ Відро́дження — the Renaissance.

blocks.p: Not quite afternoon, not yet evening: the soft time when the light turns golden and the day starts slowing down. English has *dusk* and *twilight*, but those come later.

example.a: Надвечі́р'я — мій улю́блений час для прогу́лянок.
example.b: The late afternoon, just before evening, is my favourite time for walks.

blocks.p: A noun for something that tastes wonderful, said with feeling. It works as a whole sentence.
Ukrainians say this before anyone eats, the way the French say *bon appétit*. English has no native phrase for it, which is why English speakers borrow the French one.

sections.h2: A word with a story: гарбу́з

blocks.h3: 12. Да́ти гарбуза́ (dáty harbuzá) — to turn down a suitor

blocks.p: *Гарбуз* is simply a pumpkin. But in the old Ukrainian matchmaking tradition, a girl who didn't want to marry a suitor gave him — or his matchmakers — a pumpkin instead of an answer. The idiom lives on: *to give someone a pumpkin* means to reject them.

example.note: Гарбуза is the genitive-style object form used in this idiom.

blocks.p: These ones do translate, but I can't leave them out. They are the words I keep coming back to as a poet:

list: **Натхне́ння** (natkhnénnya) — inspiration. Doesn't it sound exactly like what it means?
**Мрі́я** (mríya) — a dream, the kind you wish for. It was also the name of the An-225, the world's largest cargo plane, built in Ukraine.
**Тепло́** (tepló) — warmth, of the sun and of people. I think it's one of the most beautiful words in any language.

sections.h2: How to learn words like these

blocks.p: Untranslatable words are best learnt the way Ukrainians learn them: in context. Learn a phrase, not a single word — *туга за домом*, *жага до життя*, *рідна мова* — and notice when people use it in songs, films and conversation.

blocks.tip: Keep a page in your notebook for words that don't translate. For each one, write the Ukrainian sentence where you met it, not an English equivalent. You'll feel the meaning long before you can define it.

blocks.p: If you want to hear words like these used naturally — and start using them yourself — that's exactly what we do in my [Ukrainian lessons online](/services/ukrainian-lessons). New to the language? Start with my [guide to learning Ukrainian](/learn/how-to-learn-ukrainian).

faq.q: What is the most beautiful Ukrainian word?
faq.a: There's no official answer, but Ukrainians often name words like мрія (dream), кохання (love), тепло (warmth) and натхнення (inspiration). Many learners fall for затишок, the Ukrainian word for cosiness and calm.

faq.q: What is the difference between кохати and любити?
faq.a: Любити is the general verb for love and liking: family, friends, food, hobbies. Кохати is only for romantic love. Я тебе кохаю is what you say to a partner.
Смачного is what Ukrainians say before a meal, like bon appétit. It literally means “(I wish you something) tasty”. The usual reply is дякую, і вам — thank you, you too.

faq.q: What does it mean to give someone a pumpkin in Ukrainian?
faq.a: Дати гарбуза means to turn down a suitor. It comes from an old matchmaking custom in which a girl gave a pumpkin to a suitor she didn't want to marry.
